transcript:
This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix into your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
Tech stocks dragged down markets this week. NPR's Stephen Bissaha reports the tech-heavy NASDAQ wiped out gains for the entire year.
There was plenty of positive news from artificial intelligence companies this week.
Invidia reported earnings that easily beat Wall Street expectations, and Enthropic had a record-setting public offering Thursday.
None of that stopped a rough end of the week on the market.
Invidia's stock continued its nosedive, down about 12% for the day.
Enthropic's stock fell close to 10%. All that signals that investors are expecting an AI slowdown.
One positive sign for Thanksgiving travelers looking to drive rather than fly next week.
The national average for a gallon of gas is down to $3.68, according to AAA, a drop of about 50 cents from the start of November.
Stephen Bissaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
The Justice Department says it will oppose a request to block the Army from detonating roughly five tons of an unstable, lead-based explosive in Iowa.
This after a federal appeals court temporarily suspended the permit.
Iowa Public Radio's Tom Barton reports.
The Army moved the blast from Friday to Monday.
They could still go ahead if the court lifts its hold on the EPA permit.
Two environmental groups say the agency didn't fully consider safer ways to dispose of the explosive.
Earth Justice Attorney Tien Chao says the lead dust could cross state lines.
It does truly feel unprecedented, right?
Taking this much explosive that contains lead and to blow it up,
knowing that it is going to disperse over communities, over farmland, over water bodies.
The Army says handling the drums for chemical treatment could trigger an accidental explosion.
The court hasn't said when it will rule.
For NPR News, I'm Tom Barton in Des Moines.
The Energy Department has officially secured the money it needs to move staff into the Department of Education Building.
As NPR's Johnaki Mehta reports, this is more than just Washington bureaucracy and logistics.
It's part of a dismantling of the Education Department.
Education Secretary Linda McMahon has spent her tenure doing what she was hired to do,
breaking up her agency.
Half the staff were cut last year and hundreds of remaining employees have been scattered across Washington.
While the timeline for the actual move isn't clear,
the plan to shift energy department workers into the headquarters of the Ed Department
puts a nail in the coffin, cementing a physical dismantling of the agency.
The historic Education Building was named for Lyndon B. Johnson,
the former president and school teacher who made education programs,
like helping low-income students, central to his agenda.
Johnaki Mehta, NPR News.
Residents of Florida's Atlantic Coast along the St. John's River and the central part of the state are being warned about the possibility of flooding.
After several days of heavy rains, there could be up to 10 more inches of rain through Saturday.
This is NPR.
A second judge, this one in suburban Alexandria, Virginia,
has indefinitely blocked President Trump's plans for what he calls
"a triumphal arch just yards from the back of the Lincoln Memorial and near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery."
Previously, a judge in Washington, D.C., extended an order blocking the construction,
which preservation and veterans groups say would cause irreparable harm to the D.C. area and the suburbs.
The Kansas City Chiefs' wheelchair football team is just one game away from a three-peat.
As Frank Morris of member station WCUR reports, the Chiefs play for their third consecutive
championship Saturday against their arch rival, the wheelchair Chicago Bears.
The Chiefs have been dominant in the 15-member USA Wheelchair Football League since the beginning.
They played in all five championship games, beating the wheelchair Bears in the last two.
League commissioner Carolyn Lee says it's always a grudge match.
They are very closely matched. It's a really unique rivalry here, and it's really going to be a fun game.
The Chiefs have the home field advantage, but the wheelchair Bears have a new weapon,
a former Chiefs standout who moved for work and signed on with the Bears.
For NPR News, I'm Frank Morris in Kansas City.
With a 3 a.m. Eastern Time deadline looming, Union security watchmen who guard the giant ports
at Los Angeles and Long Beach could be on strike Saturday.
The guards represented by the ILWU have been negotiating with management for more than a year.
I'm Dan Ronan, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Tech stocks drag markets down, with NASDAQ erasing its gains for the entire year
Gas prices fall to $3.68 a gallon nationally ahead of Thanksgiving travel, per AAA
Justice Department to oppose request blocking Army's planned five-ton lead explosive detonation in Iowa
Energy Department secures funding to move staff into the Education Department building, advancing dismantling
Florida's Atlantic Coast and central regions warned of flooding from up to 10 more inches of rain
Second judge in Virginia indefinitely blocks Trump's triumphal arch project near Lincoln Memorial
Kansas City Chiefs wheelchair football team seeks third straight championship against Chicago Bears
Union security watchmen at Los Angeles and Long Beach ports could strike Saturday amid contract talks
